name: Calculating the Average of the Input Integers that are an Even Number
description: Construct a program that reads a series of integer values from the user, sums up the integers that are an even number, and calculate their average. The user enters 0 to indicate the end of the input.

comments.content: We need variable total to maintain a running total, which means the sum of the even integers that the user enters.
We need variable count to count how many even integers the user enters. This is required for calculating the average of the even integers that the user enters.
We need variable average to store the average of the even integers entered by the user.
We need to read and process the integers that the user enters. To read the input integers from the user, we need to define a Scanner object.

We can create a Scanner object using the operator new, as shown in this statement. The System.in object represents the standard input stream, which by default is the keyboard. It tells the java compiler that the input will be provided through keyboard.
We prompt the user to enter an integer. The user can enter 0 to quit.
We need to read the integer that the user enters and store it in a variable. We read the integer by calling the nextInt() method because this input is an integer.
Note that if the user provides a non-integer number, an exception will be thrown because the input type is inconsistent with the expected data type, i.e., int.

We need to process the integer that the user has entered and repeat receiving and processing the integers from the user as long as the user enters an integer that is different from 0. Therefore, we need to use a loop structure. Since we don't know ahead of time how many times the loop will be repeated, we need to use a while loop. The condition in the while loop tests whether the body of the loop should be repeated, so it should test whether the input integer is different from 0.
The body of the while loop is repeated as long as the user enters an integer that is different from 0. The loop terminates when the loop condition evaluates to false, that is when the user enters 0.

We want to calculate the average of the even numbers that the user enters. Therefore, we should skip numbers that aren't even. To do this, we need an if statement that uses the remainder (%) operator to test whether the integer that the user entered is even. The even integer must be divisible by 2 i.e. when it is divided by 2, there is a zero remainder.
The body of this if statement is executed only if the integer is even, that is the remainder when the integer is divided by 2 is zero. Note that the % operator returns the remainder of the division.

We have to count the number of even integers that are entered because we need it for calculating the average of even integers. Therefore, each time that the user enters an even integer, we need to increment the number of even integers that user has entered by 1. Note that if the user enters 0, it will not be counted.

The increment operator (++) adds 1 to the value of variable count and the result is stored back into the variable count. Therefore, it is functionally equivalent to the statement count = count + 1. Note that the two plus signs that make up the operator cannot be separated by white space.
We need to add the even integer that the user has entered to the running total. So, each time that the user enters an even integer, that integer needs to be added to and stored back into total.

The += operator adds the value on the right-hand side of the assignment operator (i.e., value of variable num) to the current value of the variable on the left-hand side (i.e., value of variable total) and the result is stored in the variable total. Thus, this statement is equivalent to the statement total = total + num.

Each time the body of the while loop is repeated, the sum and the number of the even integers that the user has entered will be printed to the default standard output stream. We do this to see how sum and count are updated after each repeat of the loop. The printed text is followed by the end-of-line character at the end.
The expression in the argument of the println method returns a string that is obtained by concatenating the given strings and value of the variables.
We prompt the user to enter the next integer. Similar to the previous case, 0 indicates the end of the input.

We need to read the next integer that the user enters but this needs to be done only after we have added the previous even integer to the running total and we updated the count. Therefore, the next integer must be read in the end of the loop body. If we read the next number in the beginning of the loop body, then if first integer that the user has entered is even, it would not be added to the sum or counted which will result in an incorrect calculation of the sum and average.
We read the integer by calling the nextInt() method because this input is an integer.
Note that if the user provides a non-integer number, an exception will be thrown because the input type is inconsistent with the expected data type, i.e., int.
We close the scanner as we do not want to process any input from the user in the rest of the program.

We need the if statement at the end of the program to avoid a divide-by-zero error. This occurs if the user does not enter any even integer.

To determine if the divide-by-zero error would occur, we need to test if the number of even integers entered by the user is equal to zero.
If the number of even integers that the user has entered is equal to zero, then the body of this if statement gets executed. Otherwise, the body of this if statement is skipped.
This statement prints to the default standard output stream that no even integers were entered. This text is followed by the end-of-line character at the end.

If the above if test fails (i.e., when the number of even integers the the user has entered is different from zero), we could calculate the average by dividing the sum by the number of even integers entered by the user.

We need to calculate the average by dividing the sum of the even integers by the number of the even integers that the user entered. Notice that both variables in the division are int and dividing an int by an int results in an int. Since we want to keep the fractional part, we need to cast one of the operands to a floating-point data type like double. When floating-point value total is divided by an integer value count, the value of count is promoted to a floating-point value automatically, before the division takes place; thus, producing a floating-point result.

We want to round the average to three decimal places. To do this, we need to instantiate a DecimalFormat object with a pattern. In this statement, the pattern defined by the string 0.### indicates that at least one digit should be printed to the left of the decimal point and should be a zero if the integer portion of the value is zero. It also indicates that the fractional portion of the value should be rounded to three digits.

This statement prints the calculated average to the default standard output stream. Note that the average is formatted to have maximum of three decimal places. The printed text is followed by the end-of-line character at the end.
The expression in the argument of the println method returns a string that is obtained by concatenating the given string and value of the formatted variable.
